title: The Latter Glory and the Signet Ring
summary: Haggai brings three more messages in the autumn and winter of 520 BC. The first comforts builders who think the new temple looks like nothing, promising that God will shake the nations and fill the house with a glory greater than the former. The second uses two questions about ritual purity to show that a defiled people defile what they offer, and promises blessing from the day the foundation is laid. The third tells Zerubbabel that God will overturn the thrones of the nations and make him like a signet ring.
story: In Haggai 1 the prophet rebuked the returned exiles for living in finished houses while God's house lay in ruins, and within about three weeks the governor, the high priest, and the people began to work. This chapter picks up a month later, when the first enthusiasm has met a hard fact: what they are building is small and plain. Haggai's three messages answer three troubles in turn: discouragement at how little the work looks, the question of whether a sacrifice offered by an unclean people can please God, and the empty throne of David. Two months after Haggai's first message, his colleague Zechariah began to prophesy (Zechariah 1:1), and the temple would be finished in 515 BC (Ezra 6:15). With this chapter the book of Haggai ends, looking forward to a shaking of the whole world.
historical:
The dates are precise. The first message came on the twenty-first day of the seventh month (verse 1), about mid-October 520 BC, and the second and third on the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month (verses 10 and 20), about mid-December of the same year, all in the second year of Darius I of Persia. The twenty-first of the seventh month was the last day of the Feast of Booths, Israel's autumn harvest festival (Leviticus 23:34-36), the same festival at which Solomon had dedicated the first temple (1 Kings 8:2). A thin harvest and a half-built temple would have made the contrast painful.

Judah was then a small province in the Persian Empire. Its governor, Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, was a grandson of Jehoiachin, the king of Judah taken to Babylon in 597 BC, so the royal line of David lived on in him, though he ruled for the Persian king and not as a king. Darius had only recently put down a wave of revolts across the empire after taking the throne in 522 BC. Talk of God shaking thrones and overturning kingdoms was not abstract. Ezra 3:12 records that when the foundations were first laid years earlier, older people who had seen Solomon's temple wept aloud, and Haggai's question in verse 3 speaks to that same memory. The first temple had been destroyed about sixty-six years before this chapter.
cultural:
The middle message turns on Israel's laws of holiness and impurity. In the law, some things were holy (set apart to God, like the meat of a sacrifice) and some were unclean (ritually unfit for worship, such as a person who had touched a dead body, Numbers 19:11-13). Haggai asks the priests, whose job was to give rulings on such questions (Leviticus 10:10-11), for torah, instruction. Does holy meat carried in the fold of a robe make other food holy when the robe touches it? No; holiness did not pass on that way at second hand. Does a person defiled by a corpse make food unclean by touching it? Yes. Impurity spread more easily than holiness. Haggai then applies the ruling: the people themselves are unclean before God, so their offerings are unclean too, however holy the altar.

The last message uses the image of a signet ring. In the ancient Near East a signet was a seal worn on the finger or on a cord, pressed into clay or wax to authorize documents in the owner's name. To be someone's signet was to carry his authority. The image recalls Jeremiah 22:24, where God said that even if Jehoiachin (called Coniah) were the signet ring on his right hand, he would tear him off. Haggai uses the same picture to say that God has taken Jehoiachin's grandson back into his hand.
literary: The chapter holds three dated oracles, each opened with the formula that the word of the LORD came through Haggai. The first (verses 1-9) is a message of encouragement built on a triple command, be strong, addressed to the governor, the priest, and the people, and on a series of promises closed repeatedly with the title the LORD of Hosts. The second (verses 10-19) is a prophetic lesson built on questions and answers, like a legal case, followed by a call repeated three times to consider carefully. The third (verses 20-23) is a short royal oracle to Zerubbabel. The book is framed by the people's poverty and neglect in chapter 1 and the promise of shaking, glory, and blessing here.

outline.t: Be strong and work, for I am with you
The nations shaken and the latter glory of the house
A ruling from the priests: an unclean people
From this day on I will bless you
Zerubbabel as the LORD's signet ring

doctrines.note: The priests' ruling teaches that impurity spreads more readily than holiness, and that holy things do not make an unclean people clean. God's presence and blessing are not secured by a building or a ritual; the people themselves must be made clean.
God grounds his command to work in his promise from the exodus and in the assurance that his Spirit remains among them (verse 5). The strength to build is his presence, not the size of the project.

God will shake heaven, earth, and nations and overturn royal thrones. The small temple and the powerless governor are placed inside a larger claim: the kingdoms of the world are not permanent, and God's purposes for his house and his chosen servant will outlast them.

words.note: Kavod, glory. The root has the sense of weight or heaviness, and so of honor and splendor. In the exodus and at Solomon's dedication, the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle and the temple (Exodus 40:34; 1 Kings 8:11). Haggai uses the word for the former splendor the old people remember and for the greater glory God promises to this humble house.

Chemdah, a desirable or precious thing. In verse 7 it is usually translated as the treasures or wealth of the nations, which fits the next verse's word about silver and gold. Older translations such as the King James Version rendered it the desire of all nations and read it as a title for the Messiah. The grammar favors the treasures of the nations, but the passage was still read with Christ in view.

Raash, to shake or quake. The verb is used for earthquakes and for the trembling of creation when God appears, as at Sinai. Here God says he will shake heaven and earth and all the nations, the kind of upheaval that brings down empires and brings their treasures to God's house.

Chotam, a seal or signet. It was the owner's personal mark, carried carefully and used to sign in his name. Calling Zerubbabel a signet reverses the rejection of his grandfather in Jeremiah 22:24 and marks him as chosen and authorized by God.

christ: The New Testament picks up two threads of this chapter. Hebrews 12:26-27 quotes God's promise to shake the heavens and the earth once more and reads it as the final shaking in which everything that can be shaken is removed, so that a kingdom that cannot be shaken remains, the kingdom believers receive through Christ. And Zerubbabel appears in both genealogies of Jesus (Matthew 1:12-13; Luke 3:27), so the chosen signet ring of verse 23 stands in the line through which the promise to David ran to Jesus. Zerubbabel himself never wore a crown, and the thrones of the nations were not overturned in his day; Christians read the promise as reaching past him to the Son of David who is the true King. The promise of a greater glory in this house has also been read in light of Jesus's teaching in its courts, since the second temple, rebuilt and enlarged by Herod, was the temple he entered. The link here is one of fulfillment through the line and the kingdom rather than a prediction spelled out in the text.

hard.q: How was the latter glory of this house greater than the former, when the second temple never matched Solomon's?
hard.a:
The difficulty is real. The second temple began small, lacked the ark of the covenant, and later tradition noted that no cloud of glory filled it at its dedication as it had filled Solomon's. Herod the Great began a vast rebuilding around 20 or 19 BC that made it one of the famous buildings of the Roman world, but that is not quite what Haggai promised either, and the temple was destroyed in AD 70.

Interpreters answer in several ways. Many Jewish and Christian readers take the promise as fulfilled in part by the wealth and honor the temple later drew from the nations, and look for its completion in the age to come. Christian interpreters have commonly seen the greater glory in the presence of Jesus himself, who taught in its courts and spoke of his body as the temple (John 2:19-21), and in the New Testament's picture of God's people as his temple and of a city whose temple is the Lord (Revelation 21:22). Others stress that prophetic promises often describe the goal of God's work rather than the next stage of it. On any reading, the chapter's point for the first builders was that the size of what they could see was not the measure of what God would do with it.

questions: The older people compared the new temple with the memory of the old and saw nothing. Where does comparison with the past keep you from doing the work in front of you?
Haggai teaches that holiness does not rub off on an unclean people by contact with holy things. What does that say about trusting in religious activity or surroundings?
God promised Zerubbabel a future that he did not see in his lifetime. How do you hold a promise whose fulfillment may reach past you?
